Fretboard notes

Find your notes, one string at a time.

A fret is one semitone. The same note appears in several places: use the open strings and the 12th fret as landmarks.

Try it on the fretboard ↗

Understand

Read the tuning from left to right in a chord diagram. In the horizontal diagrams, the first string in that tuning is at the bottom. At fret 12, a string sounds one octave above its open note.

Standard high-G tuning: G C E A. The G string is higher than C and E; the string order is not a low-to-high pitch order.

Make the connection

There are twelve pitch classes before the names repeat. From C: C C♯ D D♯ E F F♯ G G♯ A A♯ B. Enharmonic names such as C♯ and D♭ share a pitch in this tuning. At fret 12 the name repeats, but the sound is an octave higher, not the identical pitch.

Play it

Find every pink A in the diagram. Say the string and fret before playing. Hide the picture and find three of them again.

Say the note name before playing each number. In the second pass, name the destination before moving your hand. Then choose one note at random and find it on a second string. Use the diagram to check your answer rather than counting from zero every time.

Four lines, from top to bottom: A E C g. The lowercase g marks high G, not the lowest pitch. These examples use high-G GCEA; baritone DGBE needs different positions.

A worked example

Read left to right. Counts above mark the beats; numbers on the lines are frets; numbers below give the duration in beats. R = rest. Stacked fret numbers sound together. Start at 60 BPM.

Read the example as text
  1. Bar 1
    1. String 3 (C), Fret 0, C · 1 beats
    2. String 3 (C), Fret 2, D · 1 beats
    3. String 3 (C), Fret 4, E · 1 beats
    4. String 3 (C), Fret 5, F · 1 beats
  2. Bar 2
    1. String 2 (E), Fret 0, E · 1 beats
    2. String 2 (E), Fret 1, F · 1 beats
    3. String 2 (E), Fret 3, G · 1 beats
    4. String 2 (E), Fret 5, A · 1 beats

A mistake to avoid

Treating B–C or E–F as a two-fret gap puts every following note one fret out. Fret markers are landmarks, not note names; their notes depend on the string.

Listen and check

Between B and C, and between E and F, there is only one fret. There are two frets between the other adjacent natural notes.

Ready for the next step?

Name four random positions correctly, including one open string and one above fret 5. Find the same note name an octave higher and listen to the relationship.
